newsitem.title: USA: A new Postal ad campaign hits private competitors.
newsitem.headline: A new Postal ad campaign hits private competitors.

text.p: In one of those rare cases in which a federal agency is competing with private industry, the United States Postal Service has been running a series of television commercials promoting its Priority Mail as cheaper and more efficient than the major private delivery services.

United Parcel Service and Federal Express Corporation are in a stew about it. UPS Chairman Kent Nelson told a House subcommittee that the 30-second commercials are "appalling" and a UPS spokesman called them misleading.
Federal Express said it has complained about the commercials to the TV networks, also called them inaccurate and hinted, through a spokeman, of some near-future "response in the marketplace."

However, Fred Brennan, spokesman for the Postal Service in Washington, said the television advertising was intended to increase business and has done so to the extent of "a strong 10 percent in Priority Mail over last year."
He said he disagreed with the complaints and added that "we intend to continue this sort of advertising."
The commercials, appearing on both local and national TV beginning early in March, are "a premiere campaign for us in building a brand identity," he said.
The Post Office, which operates under congressional oversight and has a board of governors appointed by the president, competes head-on with the two delivery giants.
They say it's not a level playing field because the Post Office has the "protection" of the federal government, doesn't pay taxes and can borrow directly from the Treasury.

The two companies, on the other hand, are responsible to shareholders, pay taxes and have to negotiate with banks for financing. Should a government agency compete head-to-head with private industry? UPS and Fedex say an emphatic "No."

The Post Office "tries to be competitive," said Brennan. "But sometimes we find ourselves locked in. We can't offer volume discounts as UPS and Fedex can. We aren't allowed to make a profit. We can only fund ourselves from stamps and deliveries."
"Why is UPS complaining? They already have the lion's share of parcel post," he said. "They even lobby to keep our rates up so that they can keep their's high."
UPS' Nelson called the Post Office promotion "unfair competition" in testimony before the Subcommittee on Postal Reform of the House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight.

"Private companies shouldn't have to compete unfairly with a federal agency," he said. "The Post Office Service already has a monopoly on first-class mail which it can use to subsidise other services."
Although Fedex Chairman Frederick Smith also testified before the committee, he did not refer to the Post Office commercials.

Greg Rossiter, Fedex director of public relations, said from Memphis that "although we did write to the networks about the commercials, we looked at other options but found them limited because the Post Office enjoys the protection of the government. We are concerned about many inaccuracies in the commercials. But we prefer to respond in the marketplace."
In Atlanta, UPS spokesperson Gina Ellrich said "the commercials are misleading. Our deliveries are tracked and guaranteed, the Post Office's aren't. And that is important to the consumer."

She added that UPS has not undertaken any formal rebuttal and has no advertising campaign planned to do so. "But we have been aggressive about talkng about it, particularly our chairman in testifying before the subcommittee."

The Post Office commercials compared the agency's priority mail rates with those of the two private companies, saying the Post Office rates were lower. They also claimed that the agency had more delivery trucks and airplanes for fast delivery than the private sector.
But Fedex's spokesman, Greg Rossiter, scoffed at those claims and others in the commercials.
"The Post Office doesn't even have its own aircraft. Federal Express has the largest fleet of aircraft, 560 planes which deliver our shipments," he said.
After intimating that Fedex might take some market action, Rossiter would only say, "Talk to us in about two weeks."
And so goes the flap in the government vs. industry contretemps. Stay tuned.
